name: Judges
v: Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal, went to Shechem — to his mother's brothers and the whole clan of his mother's family — and made his pitch:
"Ask every man of Shechem this: what's better for you — seventy men, all sons of Jerubbaal, ruling over you, or one man? And remember — I'm your bone and your blood."
His mother's brothers carried the message to the leaders of Shechem, word for word. And their hearts swung toward Abimelech. They said, "He's our brother."
So they handed him seventy pieces of silver out of the temple of Baal-Berith, and Abimelech used it to hire a crew of reckless, worthless men who followed him wherever he went.
He marched to his father's house in Ophrah and slaughtered his brothers — Jerubbaal's seventy sons — on a single stone. Only Jotham, the youngest, survived. He had hidden himself.
Then all the leaders of Shechem and the whole house of Millo gathered at the oak by the pillar in Shechem and crowned Abimelech king.
Word reached Jotham. He climbed to the top of Mount Gerizim, lifted his voice, and shouted down to them: "Listen to me, men of Shechem — and may God listen to you.
Once the trees set out to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'
But the olive tree answered, 'Should I give up my rich oil — by which gods and men are honored — just to sway above the trees?'
So the trees said to the fig, 'You come and reign over us.'
But the fig tree said, 'Should I abandon my sweetness, my excellent fruit, just to sway above the trees?'
So the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.'
And the vine said, 'Should I forsake my wine — the joy of gods and men — just to sway above the trees?'
Then all the trees said to the thornbush, 'You come and reign over us.'
And the thornbush told the trees: 'If you're truly anointing me king over you, then come — take shelter in my shade. But if not — let fire come out of the thornbush and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'
So now — if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, if you've treated Jerubbaal and his house well, if you've given him what his hands deserved —
my father fought for you, threw his life on the line, and rescued you from Midian's grip.

But today you've risen up against my father's house. You butchered his sons — seventy men on one stone — and crowned Abimelech, son of his slave-girl, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he's your brother.
If today you've acted in good faith and integrity toward Jerubbaal and his house — then enjoy Abimelech, and may he enjoy you.
But if not — let fire blaze out of Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and the house of Millo, and let fire blaze out of the leaders of Shechem and the house of Millo and consume Abimelech."
Then Jotham bolted. He fled to Beer and settled there, beyond the reach of his brother Abimelech.
Abimelech ruled Israel for three years.
Then God sent a poisonous spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem turned on Abimelech —

so that the violence done to Jerubbaal's seventy sons would come home, their blood landing on Abimelech, their brother who killed them, and on the leaders of Shechem who put the strength in his hand to do it.
The leaders of Shechem set ambushers in the hills against him, robbing everyone who passed by on the road. Word reached Abimelech.
Then Gaal son of Ebed arrived in Shechem with his brothers — and the leaders of Shechem put their trust in him.
They went out into the fields, gathered the grapes, trod them, and threw a festival. They entered the temple of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

And Gaal son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Isn't he the son of Jerubbaal? And isn't Zebul his deputy? Serve the men of Hamor, Shechem's father — why should we serve Abimelech?
If only this people were under my hand — I'd get rid of Abimelech." Then he sent word to Abimelech: "Beef up your army and come out."
When Zebul, the ruler of the city, heard Gaal son of Ebed's words, his anger flared.
He sent messengers to Abimelech in secret: "Look — Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem, and they're stirring up the city against you.
So get up tonight, you and your men, and lie in ambush in the fields.
In the morning, the moment the sun rises, charge the city. When Gaal and his men come out against you, do to him whatever your hand finds to do."
So Abimelech rose by night, his whole force with him, and they set ambushes against Shechem in four companies.
Gaal son of Ebed walked out and stood at the entrance of the city gate. And Abimelech rose from his ambush — he and his men with him.
When Gaal saw them he said to Zebul, "Look — people are coming down from the mountain peaks." Zebul replied, "You're seeing the shadows of the mountains as if they were men."
Gaal spoke again: "Look — people are coming down from the navel of the land, and another company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."
Then Zebul said to him, "Where's your big mouth now? You said, 'Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?' Aren't these the people you mocked? Go on — go out and fight them."
So Gaal marched out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and Gaal ran. Many fell wounded, all the way to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech stayed in Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out — they could no longer live in Shechem.
The next day the people went out to the fields. Word reached Abimelech.
He took his men, split them into three companies, and set an ambush in the fields. When he saw the people leaving the city, he sprang up and struck them down.
Abimelech and the company with him rushed forward and took position at the entrance of the city gate. The other two companies charged everyone in the fields and cut them down.
All that day Abimelech fought against the city. He captured it, killed everyone in it, demolished the city, and salted the ground.
When the leaders of the tower of Shechem heard, they took refuge in the stronghold of the temple of El-Berith.
Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the tower of Shechem had gathered there.
So Abimelech climbed Mount Zalmon with all his men. He took an axe, cut a branch from a tree, hoisted it on his shoulder, and said to his men, "What you've seen me do — hurry, do the same."

So every man cut his own branch, and they followed Abimelech. They piled the branches against the stronghold and set the place on fire over the heads of those inside. Everyone in the tower of Shechem died — about a thousand men and women.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez, camped against it, and seized it.
But there was a strong tower in the middle of the city, and all the men and women — all the city's leaders — fled there, locked themselves in, and climbed up to the roof.
Abimelech reached the tower, attacked it, and approached the entrance to burn it down.
Then a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.
He called to his young armor-bearer in a rush: "Draw your sword and kill me — don't let them say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" The young man ran him through, and he died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they each went home.
So God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech — what he had done to his father by murdering his seventy brothers.
And all the wickedness of the men of Shechem — God brought it back on their own heads. The curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal landed.

com.d:
# Judges 9: The Tragedy of Ambition Without God

When power becomes an end in itself rather than a stewardship from God, it corrupts everything it touches—this is the haunting lesson of Abimelech's brutal rise and fall.

Abimelech's story begins with a crime that seems promising: he murders his seventy brothers and claims kingship through manipulation and ruthlessness. His success appears swift. Yet the text reveals something more tragic than his ambition alone—it shows how communities decline when they forget the God who judges. Even Jotham's prophetic parable, comparing Abimelech to a worthless bramble offered the throne, falls on ears too eager for human leadership to hear divine warning. What follows is a domino effect of violence: Abimelech's own subjects eventually turn against him, civil war breaks out, and he dies in humiliation, crushed by a woman dropping a millstone from a tower. The narrative closes with brutal irony—the man who seized power through fratricide meets his end through cowardice, unwilling to bear the shame of being defeated by a woman.

This passage confronts us with hard truths about ambition. When we pursue position, influence, or success outside of God's calling, we plant seeds that inevitably produce conflict and emptiness. The tragedy isn't just Abimelech's—it's shared by Shechem's citizens who supported him, who were eventually destroyed by the very leader they'd chosen. Their complicity in evil bore its own consequences.

We live in a world that rewards Abimelech's methods: strategic ruthlessness, image management, the willingness to eliminate competitors. But Scripture warns that this path leads not to lasting peace but to a house divided, burning from within. True leadership comes through alignment with God's purposes, not against them. Our ambitions matter most when they're surrendered to God's design.

Where are you tempted to seize power or position outside of God's calling? What would it look like to trust Him with your influence instead?
com.s:
Judges 9 presents one of the most complex and theologically significant narratives in the Deuteronomistic History, recounting Abimelech's violent rise to power and subsequent downfall. This chapter stands in deliberate contrast to the preceding account of Gideon, who refused kingship (8:22–23), while his illegitimate son Abimelech aggressively seizes it through fratricide and political manipulation. The setting centers on Shechem, a city of profound patriarchal significance located between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where Abimelech's Canaanite maternal connections provide him entry into local power structures.

The chapter's literary centerpiece is Jotham's fable (vv. 7–15), the oldest known fable in biblical literature and one of only two true fables in the Hebrew canon. The Hebrew term *mashal* encompasses this parabolic discourse, wherein productive trees—the olive, fig, and vine—refuse kingship because meaningful work surpasses empty honor. Only the worthless bramble (*atad*) accepts, offering shade it cannot provide while threatening destruction it can deliver. This brilliant political satire exposes the nature of tyrannical rule: those who seek power most aggressively are least qualified to wield it beneficially.

The theological framework emerges through the concept of divine retribution. The narrator explicitly attributes the discord between Abimelech and Shechem to God sending "an evil spirit" (*ruach ra'ah*) between them (v. 23), language paralleling 1 Samuel 16:14. This raises interpretive questions about divine sovereignty and human culpability that scholars continue to debate. The term *gemul* (recompense/retribution) appears in Jotham's closing curse (v. 57), establishing that the subsequent violence represents deserved judgment rather than random chaos.

The chapter's gruesome conclusion—Abimelech's skull crushed by a millstone thrown by a woman, followed by his shame-driven request for death by sword—demonstrates the Deuteronomistic conviction that covenant violation and bloodguilt inevitably produce destruction. Within the broader canonical context, this narrative functions as an anti-monarchical polemic, anticipating tensions that will resurface in 1 Samuel 8–12. The cyclical violence previews Israel's political instability while affirming that legitimate authority derives from divine designation rather than human ambition or violence.
com.p:
This dark chapter unfolds approximately 1150 years before Christ's advent, during the troubled era of the judges when Israel had no king and "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." The period of the judges represents a recurring cycle of apostasy, oppression, repentance, and deliverance—a time when God raised up deliverers to rescue His people yet Israel perpetually failed to learn faithfulness. Within the grand arc of redemption, this passage stands between the Exodus deliverance and the establishment of the Davidic kingdom, exposing the catastrophic void of godly leadership and foreshadowing Israel's desperate need for a righteous King.

Abimelech, the illegitimate son of Gideon by a Shechemite concubine, embodies the anti-king, the murderous usurper who seizes power through treachery rather than divine appointment. His slaughter of seventy brothers upon a single stone presents a horrifying inversion of the sacrificial altar—instead of animals offered to God, human blood is shed to satisfy ambition. This massacre stands as a dark type pointing by contrast to Christ: where Abimelech killed his brothers to gain a throne, Christ the true King laid down His own life to give His brothers an inheritance. Where Abimelech's three-year reign brought only bloodshed and curse, Christ's eternal reign brings healing and blessing to the nations.

Jotham's parable of the trees stands as Scripture's first recorded parable and carries enduring prophetic weight. The worthy trees—the olive, fig, and vine—refuse the crown, unwilling to abandon their fruitful service, while the worthless bramble eagerly accepts with threats of consuming fire. This pattern repeats throughout history: those grasping for power prove least worthy of it, while true servants often resist prominence. The parable prophetically indicts all human kingdoms built on violence and self-exaltation, anticipating Christ who came not to be served but to serve.

The chapter's conclusion—Abimelech's ignominious death by a millstone dropped by a woman, and the mutual destruction of Shechem's conspirators—demonstrates God's sovereign justice operating even through human wickedness. The curse of Jotham finds literal fulfillment, revealing that divine retribution, though sometimes delayed, remains certain.

For the church dwelling between Christ's advents, Judges 9 warns against the spirit of Abimelech that lurks wherever leaders grasp for power rather than wash feet, wherever ambition masquerades as anointing. It deepens our longing for the returning King whose reign shall know no end and whose kingdom operates by cruciform love rather than consuming fire.
